catalog_quote: [Wheeler 1988:251] Except in Nice and varieties in Italy where, e.g. mànega 'sleeve', diménegue 'Sunday', 'parla-li 'speak to him', are to be found, Occitan shuns proparoxytones, and shifts stress to a following syllable, to give, for example, paroxytonic lagrema 'tear', persegue 'peach', silaba 'syllable', classica 'classical (f.)', credula 'credulous (f.)'. Unless a final consonant is an inflectional morpheme (e.g. joves 'young people', dison 'they say', cantàvam 'we sang') consonant-final paroxytones are rare. Many have become vowel-final through elision of the final consonant, as in conóisser 'to recognise', Antíbol 'Antibes', àngel 'angel', crèdit 'credit'; while masculine nominals have undergone stress shift by analogy with the related feminine forms, e.g. classic 'classical (m.)', credul 'credulous (m.)', contemporanèu 'contemporary (m.)', filològ 'philologist (m.)'. sweep_summary: Occitan (occi1239) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Wheeler 1988:251. The 12 title hits are all one Osnabrück/UPF prosody team (Sichel-Bazin, Buthke, Meisenburg, Prieto) plus Roca 1999 and four noise hits (Gnevsheva, Williams, Saran 1899 verse rhythm, Meisenburg's review of a French prosody book). The one open item, Sichel-Bazin's 2015 dissertation (already listed, downloaded this search of works with stress in the title from CORE since TDX/UPF are bot-walled; 161 MB, saved with extracted text extract), has a dedicated section 3.2.2.3 stating contrastive final/penult stress, final stress in consonant-final words except morphological -n/-s, no proparoxytones outside Niçart/Cisalpine/colloquial Aranese, and a weight-sensitive Lemosin subsystem — this confirms and refines the catalog's classification without displacing Wheeler as deciding source. The OUP intonation chapter and Benjamins bilinguals chapter are paywalled (Crossref abstracts read: intonation/AP interference only, no placement rule). Still unread and worth acquiring if convenient: Sichel-Bazin et al. 2013 CILFR paper (Occitan prosody in Gallo-Romance context, De Gruyter) and Roca 1999 (whether it treats Occitan first-hand is unverified). searches were done via Semantic Scholar, Crossref, CORE, HAL and archive.org APIs.

new_statements.quote: Occitan has contrastive lexical stress, falling either on the last or the penult syllable (Meisenburg 2001; Schultz-Gora 1906). For example, the word pati [ˈpa.ti] (‘patio’) with penult stress contrasts with patir [pa.ˈti] (‘to suffer’) with final stress. In this sense, it resembles the majority of Romance languages, yet antepenultimate stress is not attested in the majority of Occitan dialects.16 Words ending in a consonant — except morphological -n and -s — are generally stress-final,17 but words ending in a vowel may be stressed either on the final or on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Sichel-Bazin, Rafèu. 2015. Prosodic systems in contact: Occitan and French. PhD thesis, Universität Osnabrück / Universitat Pompeu Fabra.
new_statements.locator: p. 103, §3.2.2.3 'Word stress in Occitan' (PDF page 85 of 493); fn. 16 same page: antepenultimate stress only in Niçart, Vivaroalpine of Italy, colloquial Aranese; p. 56: 'default pattern: stress on the last syllable if it is closed by a consonant, otherwise on the penult'; p. 105: Lemosin weight-sensitive two-syllable window
new_statements.reading: Stress is confined to the final two syllables; consonant-final words (excluding inflectional -n/-s) take final stress, vowel-final words take penult by default but final stress is lexically possible (contrastive); proparoxytones only in peripheral Niçart / Cisalpine / colloquial Aranese; Lemosin has a separate weight-sensitive subsystem. This is exactly the catalog's weight-hedged coding, with the same Nice/Italy caveat Wheeler gives.

sources.quote: '§ 130. — Sauf quelques cas particuliers très rares (v. § 409), notre langue n'admet l'accent que sur la dernière sillabe d'un mot ou sur l'avant-dernière.
